extracted.intended_audience: K-12 and higher-education teachers, curriculum designers, and media-literacy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for educators on core media-literacy competencies (appropriation, multitasking, distributed cognition, collective intelligence) and classroom practices to develop them through projects, games, and tool-mediated activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation: The Ability to Meaningfully Sample and Remix Media Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation is understood as a process by which students learn by taking culture apart and putting it back together; artists build on, appropriate, and transform previous cultural materials rather than producing wholly autonomous creations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and classroom implications: emphasize that creativity often emerges through sampling and remixing (examples: Homer, Shakespeare, Sistine Chapel, jazz, hip-hop, fan fiction, collage). Teach students to analyze source structures and uses, appreciate emergent meanings, and practice transformative reuse rather than mere copying. Address ethical and legal implications of repurposing media. Pedagogical examples and activities: team workshops to adapt a media property into a game and prepare a pitch (MIT model); assignments to produce critical radio broadcasts sampling songs (Sound & Spirit); projects to reimagine classics in contemporary contexts (urban Moby Dick, Huckleberry Finn game); My Pop Studio activities (designing pop stars, reediting reality-show footage, magazine layouts). Scaffolding notes: appropriation provides support for novice creators (e.g., building on existing characters lets students focus on description/exposition), increases audience and feedback, and helps students experiment with voice and identity. Anti-patterns: treating all repurposing as piracy or penalizing overt signs of repurposed content without teaching analysis and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multitasking: The Ability to Scan the Environment and Shift Focus onto Salient Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Multitasking is the skill of scanning a rich information environment, monitoring multiple stimuli, and shifting attention to salient details when appropriate; it complements focused attention rather than being its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual points: short attention spans in digital contexts may reflect adaptive skills for fast context-switching (comparisons to managers and 'hunters' vs 'farmers'). Students must learn to distinguish productive multitasking from off-task distraction and to know when to concentrate deeply versus when to scan. Pedagogical examples and practices: real-time classroom blogging by a TA to surface relevant links and cues during lectures; distributing language-learning materials to mobile devices for opportunistic practice (Brearley/iPod example); designing online-game-style homework that breaks tasks into discrete choices to be checked periodically (Cyber Nations); encourage mapping of externally stored information to reduce short-term memory load. Assessment/valuation: treat different attentional styles as context-dependent strengths; design classrooms that support multiple modes of learning and assess each style by its suitability for the task. Anti-patterns: equating multitasking with mere distraction or pathologizing short attention without contextual evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed Cognition: The Ability to Interact Meaningfully with Tools That Expand Mental Capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed cognition posits that intelligence is accomplished across brain, body, and world—relying on artifacts, tools, and social systems that externalize memory and processes; students must learn to think with and through technological and social resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core implications: teach students the affordances and limits of tools (calculators, databases, spell-checkers, expert systems) and when those tools can be trusted; view technologies as integral to cognition rather than as 'cheats.' Pedagogical examples and activities: squad-based video games that require mental maps of players and representations; augmented-reality and GPS-enabled games (Environmental Detectives) that integrate data collection with physical travel; handheld-guided historical tours comparing old photos to present views; Byline tool scaffolding journalistic structure (lead, byline) to teach conventions; classrooms that require collaboration with remote experts and use spreadsheets/databases to simulate instruments (e.g., mass spectrometer). Assessment/learning goals: prioritize learning how to act within distributed knowledge systems (generate, evaluate, interpret, deploy data) over rote content memorization. Design note: use new technologies to create activities that enable engagement with more complex problem domains; offloading routine computation frees students for higher-level strategic thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective Intelligence: The Ability to Pool Knowledge and Compare Notes with Others toward a Common Goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective intelligence denotes the social production of knowledge in networked communities—where individuals contribute partial expertise that the group aggregates to solve complex problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical framing: based on Pierre Lévy's idea that 'everyone knows something, nobody knows everything'—knowledge can be pooled and tapped by communities. Classroom and project examples: fan-created guides (Matrix, Pokémon) that aggregate distributed expertise; large-scale collaborative games and alternate-reality puzzles (I Love Bees, Cloudmakers) that required mass coordination and skill-sharing; civic uses such as crowdsourced mapping after Hurricane Katrina and collaborative investigation (tracking campaign finances, local crimes). Pedagogical implications: foster participation in knowledge communities, design tasks that require ad-hoc team problem solving, provide mechanisms for newcomers to be trained by peers, and emphasize teamwork as a core skill aligned with contemporary workplace ad-hocracies. Outcomes and values: builds confidence to tackle problems collectively, enables real-world impact, and reframes problem solving as collaborative rather than strictly individual.
